articles.title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B
articles.raw_description: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B brings substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution to the same 5.9 GB footprint. LAUNCH 1001011100 001011 110 Back to all posts Introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B: Powering Agentic Coding and Private Knowledge Work November 24, 2026 • PrismML Today, we’re introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution. Based on Qwen3.8 27B, it retains the previous release’s 5.9 GB model footprint while significantly improving the capabilities developers need to build agents that work with private files and tools on-device. The result is by far the strongest AI model of its memory footprint for agentic workloads. With Ternary Bonsai 2 27B , we brought stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool use to local devices. Since then, we’ve focused on making the model more effective across long sequences of tool calls: interpreting results, adjusting when a step fails, and maintaining the task’s objective through the whole interaction. This release also continues our work to make Bonsai more practical by addressing excessive thinking and repetitive loops in the previous model. Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 completes tasks in fewer turns, uses fewer tokens, and delivers results faster and more accurately. articles.title: PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches
articles.raw_description: A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson. A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson. Left. One phrase in the hands of 21 writers who were held out of training. The model read one to three real words by each of them and carried on in their hand. Right. Drawings from typed prompts. I picked these by eye from the best third of the samples; there are unpicked ones further down. Read the paper Get the code Download weights Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive . It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad. So here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt. Then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected. How it works The whole recipe. articles.title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed
articles.raw_description: TL;DR * Two agents running on the same inference server can reliably communicate, even if they cannot send each other messages or access the same fi… x AI Frontpage 134 Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed by Niranjan Deshpande , David Africa 19th Nov 2026 13 min read 3 134 TL;DR Two agents running on the same inference server can reliably communicate, even if they cannot send each other messages or access the same filesystem. They can do this by exploiting "side channels": mechanisms that let one model subtly affect another model's computation . Here, I discuss two communication protocols: Step Sizing and KV Cache Message Board . These both convey information through the way vLLM chooses kernels for particular engine steps. I show that these communication protocols work in two setups: In a color guessing game , Model A (Alice) chooses one out of 8 colors. Model B (Bob) correctly guesses Alice's color in 1,221/1,221 rounds, even though they cannot directly communicate. [1] In an untrusted monitoring protocol , a policy signals to a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot. Accordingly, the monitor lets through 354/354 "attacks" while catching 85–92% of honeypots. My initial setups are quite contrived: I tell the models the protocol and fine-tune them to detect signals. articles.title: I've been drinking wine in my kitchen
articles.raw_description: See I don’t even like alcohol much. Like, I’ll have a half-glass of wine at a fancy dinner if everyone else is having some, or one beer at a reception, but that’s it. These days, … Shtetl-Optimized The Blog of Scott Aaronson If you take nothing else from this blog: quantum computers won't solve hard problems instantly by just trying all solutions in parallel. « Moar Videos and Links I’ve been drinking wine in my kitchen See I don’t even like alcohol much. Like, I’ll have a half-glass of wine at a fancy dinner if everyone else is having some, or one beer at a reception, but that’s it. These days, though, can you blame me? Yesterday, as you all probably saw, hot on the heels of its proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, Anthropic released a proof of Valiant’s VP≠VNP conjecture —a central algebraic analogue of the P≠NP conjecture, and considered a “warmup” to proving P≠NP since the late 1970s. Then, later the same day, OpenAI released a proof of the VP≠VNP conjecture as well. You can read all about the VP vs. VNP problem in Section 6.5 of my P vs. NP survey . But briefly, for those tuning in from home, Valiant’s conjecture says that the permanent of an n×n matrix has no algebraic circuits (that is, circuits built out of addition and multiplication gates and constants) of size polynomial in n, unlike the determinant , which does. articles.title: Lua for Data Representation
articles.raw_description: july 23, 2025 lua for data representation my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format. lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]] . however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]) . the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===] , not with a ]] or a ]==] , or a ]====] . here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it: local function stringize(str) local equal_signs = "" for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do if #e >= #equal_signs then equal_signs = e .. "=" end end return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs) end of course, you can just use string.format with %q , but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code. anyway, download this file . if you want to consume massiv
